title: All is breath (Ecclesiastes 1:2)
hookLine: "vanity of vanities"; the Hebrew hevel means breath or vapor
last: THE NEED COMES FIRST, AND THE HISTORY COMES SECOND.

cards: Breathe on a cold window. A small gray cloud appears on the glass, and for a moment you could write your name in it. Then, while you watch, it shrinks from the edges and is gone.
The glass looks exactly as it did before. One book of the Tanakh takes that little cloud and holds it up to everything: work, money, wisdom, pleasure, fame, a whole lifetime.
Its opening cry is one word, said again and again. Today's word.

teach.b: Hevel. The book is Ecclesiastes, in Hebrew Kohelet, named for its speaker, the one the King James calls the Preacher.

teach.h: VANITY OF VANITIES: BREATH OF BREATHS.
teach.b: Here's how he begins: "Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity." Every vanity in that line is the same Hebrew word, hevel. And hevel isn't about pride or mirrors.
Its plain picture is breath. Vapor. The mist that rises off a cup and isn't there a moment later.
So the line can be heard another way: breath of breaths, all is breath. That changes the feeling of the book. Vanity sounds like a verdict: worthless.
Breath is real. You can feel it on your hand; it keeps you alive. It just can't be held.
Kohelet looks at everything people chase and says, again and again, hevel. You build, and someone else inherits. You grow wise, and the wise die like the foolish.
You gather, and it slips away. There's an echo here, too.
In Genesis, the brother who is killed, whom English calls Abel, is in Hebrew named Hevel. A life like a breath. Some readers find Kohelet bleak.
Others find him honest, even freeing: if everything is breath, you can stop gripping. Either way, the word asks for a light touch. Not that nothing is real, but that nothing stays in the hand.

how: Kohelet (Ecclesiastes) is one of the five scrolls of the Writings, and Ashkenazi communities read it in synagogue during the festival of Sukkot.

o: breath or vapor: real, but impossible to hold
a chain: the work that binds a person
pride: the sin of admiring yourself

games.q: all is breath — tap the pairs.

s: in Ecclesiastes, vanity means pride in your looks
the Hebrew is hevel: breath or vapor, something real that can't be held.
every 'vanity' in Ecclesiastes 1:2 is the same Hebrew word
hevel, repeated: breath of breaths, all is breath.
Abel's name in Hebrew is Hevel

games.q: you're translating Kohelet's opening cry. the word is hevel. which do you choose?
o: either; both are in the conversation.
games.why: the King James text says vanity; the Hebrew picture is breath. readers keep both in view.

practice: Breathe in through your nose, no strain, then let the breath out slowly through your mouth, longer than the breath in, and feel that you can't hold on to it and don't need to: another comes.
If a worry rises, let it ride out on the breath. If you pray, you can let one breath out carry a word of prayer.

wordCard.voice: Hevel. Breath, vapor, mist: the word the King James text renders as vanity, Kohelet's word for everything people try to hold. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: breath, vapor; the word repeated in Ecclesiastes 1:2.
